docs.title: Eyes on the Wire
docs.text:
A Practical Field Book on Deep Packet Inspection, Network Detection & Response, and the Tools That Watch the Internet · Science and Technology

How networks are inspected and watched: DPI, IDS and IPS, NDR, Zeek, Suricata, Wireshark, encrypted-traffic analysis and hands-on labs

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
This book is a friendly but technically faithful walk through the family of technologies that look inside, measure, and reason about network traffic: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), Network Detection and Response (NDR), and their close cousins (IDS, IPS, NTA, NDR, EDR, XDR, SIEM, SOAR).

Two readers are kept in mind on every page:

  • the layman, who has perhaps wondered how an internet provider knows you are streaming video, or how a corporate firewall blocks a malicious upload — and who wants to understand without drowning in jargon;

  • the undergraduate computer-science student, who needs the precise terminology, the tools, the open-source projects on GitHub, the command lines, and the techniques used in real Security Operations Centres (SOCs).

Where the topic gets technical, look for the For the Layman and For the Undergraduate side boxes; one summarises in plain language, the other adds the formal detail.

How to read it.

You can read it cover to cover, but each chapter is largely self-contained. Parts I–III lay the foundation and main concepts; Parts IV–V cover the open-source toolset; Part VI explores techniques; Part VII is hands-on; Part VIII looks ahead. Appendices collect tools, GitHub links, and a glossary.

A note on ethics.

The techniques described here can be used to defend a network and to violate privacy. The line between the two is authorisation. Inspect only traffic on networks you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor. Local laws (GDPR, India’s DPDP Act, the US Wiretap Act, etc.) impose hard limits. Chapter 30 discusses this in more depth.

docs.title: B.1 tcpdump
docs.text:
tcpdump -D                          # list interfaces
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -c 50
tcpdump -i any -w out.pcap 'port 53 or port 443'
tcpdump -r out.pcap -A 'tcp port 80'
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin) != 0'

docs.title: B.2 tshark / Wireshark filters
docs.text:
tshark -i eth0 -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
tshark -r f.pcap -q -z conv,tcp
tshark -r f.pcap -Y 'tls.handshake.extensions_server_name'

docs.title: B.3 Zeek
docs.text:
zeek -r f.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T

zkg install zeek/corelight/zeek-ja4

docs.title: Appendix C: Glossary
docs.text: BPF Berkeley Packet Filter. The kernel filtering language used by libpcap and (in its eBPF form) much modern Linux observability. Beacon A periodic, small callback from a compromised host to its command-and-control server. C2 / C&C Command and control. The infrastructure attackers use to direct compromised hosts. DGA Domain Generation Algorithm; malware generates many random domains to find a live C2. DPI Deep Packet Inspection. DPDK Data Plane Development Kit. Userspace, poll-mode packet I/O. ECH Encrypted ClientHello; hides the SNI in TLS. EDR Endpoint Detection and Response. ETA Encrypted Traffic Analysis. Flow / 5-tuple (src-ip, dst-ip, src-port, dst-port, protocol). IDS / IPS Intrusion Detection / Prevention System. IOC Indicator of Compromise; e.g., an IP, domain, hash. JA3 / JA4 TLS client fingerprint hashes. NDR Network Detection and Response. NTA Network Traffic Analysis. PCAP A packet capture file; also the library. QUIC UDP-based, TLS-integrated transport. HTTP/3 runs on it. SIEM / SOAR See Chapter on adjacent concepts. SNI Server Name Indication; the hostname inside a TLS handshake. SOC Security Operations Centre. TAP Test Access Port; a passive copy-of-traffic device. XDR eXtended Detection and Response. YARA A pattern-matching DSL for files. Zeek An open-source network analysis framework, formerly “Bro”.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Why Network Visibility Matters
docs.text:
When you open a website, send a message, join a video call, or pay a bill, a small flurry of data leaves your device and travels — through Wi-Fi, copper, fibre, satellite — to a server somewhere in the world. The reply traces its way back. To the user this looks like a single, instantaneous act. Underneath, it is a torrent of packets: tiny labelled envelopes, each carrying a slice of the conversation.

For the Layman

Imagine the internet as a vast postal network. Every letter (packet) has an address on the outside (the header) and a message on the inside (the payload). Deep Packet Inspection is what happens when a clerk along the route opens the envelope and reads the message — not just the address — to decide what to do with it. Network Detection and Response is the security guard who watches a stream of letters and recognises when something looks wrong: too many letters from one sender, an unusual time of day, a letter shaped like a hand-grenade.

For the Undergraduate

Formally, network visibility is the ability to extract, store, and reason about information from layers 2–7 of network traffic. “Shallow” inspection looks at L3–L4 headers (IP addresses, ports, flags). “Deep” inspection parses L7 (application) protocols and, increasingly, the metadata around encrypted flows: handshake fields, packet-size distributions, timing, certificate properties. Visibility tooling underpins almost every modern security control: IDS/IPS, NDR, NTA, DLP, CASB, SD-WAN policy enforcement, lawful intercept, and ISP traffic-management.

docs.title: 1.1 What this book covers
docs.text:
We will look at:

  • How a packet is constructed and how it is read by an inspector.

  • The history of DPI — from libpcap and BPF to modern L7 classifiers like nDPI.

  • The shift from intrusion detection (matching attacks) to network detection and response (continuous behavioural monitoring with playbook-driven response).

  • The open-source toolbox: Wireshark, tcpdump, Zeek, Suricata, Snort, Arkime, ntopng, Security Onion, RITA, MISP, OpenCTI, and more.

  • Detection techniques: signatures, anomaly detection, statistical and ML-based methods, encrypted-traffic fingerprints (JA3, JA4, HASSH).

  • Hands-on labs you can run on a laptop.

  • Privacy, legality, and where the technology is heading.

docs.title: 1.2 A taste: one packet, many views
docs.text:
Figure 1.1 shows a single packet as seen by progressively deeper inspectors.

Figure 1.1. One packet, seen at increasing depth.

A shallow firewall might decide based only on the L3/L4 row. A DPI engine reads the L7 row, recognises the protocol as TLS, extracts the SNI, and classifies the flow as “web browsing”. An NDR system records all of the above plus the metadata row, correlates it with thousands of other flows from the same host, and decides whether the host is acting normally.

docs.title: Chapter 2: A Quick Networking Refresher
docs.text: If you are comfortable with the OSI model, TCP/IP, and packet headers, skim this chapter; if not, read carefully — every later chapter assumes it.

docs.title: 2.1 The OSI and TCP/IP models
docs.text:
Figure 2.1. OSI vs. TCP/IP. In practice we mostly speak of L2–L7.

For the Layman

Each “layer” is a postal step. The bottom layer is the physical wire or radio. Above it is the local delivery van (Ethernet/Wi-Fi). Then the city-to-city routing (IP). Then the reliable courier service (TCP). And on top, the actual content (HTTP, video, email). DPI is concerned with the top layer; shallow inspection looks at the routing layers.

docs.title: 2.2 Anatomy of a TCP/IP packet
docs.text:
Figure 2.2. A typical TCP/IP frame on Ethernet.

A typical Ethernet frame is at most \(1518\) bytes (\(1500\) for the IP payload). Jumbo frames extend this; tunnelling protocols (GRE, VXLAN, GENEVE) wrap one frame inside another. An inspector must understand the tunnels to reach the real payload.

docs.title: 2.3 Connection-oriented vs. connectionless
docs.text:
• TCP: handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), reliable, ordered. Most observable: the three-way handshake reveals client/server roles.

  • UDP: fire-and-forget. Used by DNS, NTP, QUIC, RTP, many games. Harder to track “flows”.

  • QUIC: UDP-based, encrypted-by-default, integrates TLS 1.3. It is the elephant in the room for DPI — many fields once visible in TCP+TLS are now encrypted inside QUIC.

docs.title: 2.4 Flows, sessions, conversations
docs.text:
DPI and NDR almost always group packets into flows (often called 5-tuples: src-ip, dst-ip, src-port, dst-port, protocol). Two related unidirectional flows form a bidirectional flow (biflow).

For the Undergraduate

The classical 5-tuple is sometimes extended: VLAN/MPLS labels, VRF id, tunnel id, or a TLS session ticket can be folded in. The NetFlow/IPFIX standards (RFC 7011) define how flow records are exported from routers and probes; modern NDR systems consume IPFIX, sFlow, and direct PCAP.

docs.title: Chapter 3: What Lives Inside a Packet
3.1 Headers worth knowing by heart
docs.text:
IPv4 header (20 bytes minimum).

Key fields: Version, IHL, TOS/DSCP, Total Length, ID, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL, Protocol, Checksum, Src IP, Dst IP. The TTL alone is a goldmine: it leaks the sender’s operating system family (Linux defaults to 64, Windows to 128, some routers to 255).

TCP header (20 bytes minimum).

Key fields: Sport, Dport, Seq, Ack, Flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG, ECE, CWR), Window, Options (MSS, SACK, Timestamps, Window Scale). The Options ordering is part of the famous p0f fingerprint and lets a passive observer guess the OS without sending a single byte.

TLS handshake fields.

The ClientHello message is plaintext even in TLS 1.3 (until encrypted ClientHello / ECH is adopted). It carries the SNI (server hostname), the cipher list, the supported groups, the ALPN list, and the extension order — all of which combine into the JA3 or JA4 fingerprint.

docs.title: 3.2 The payload: the prize
docs.text:
For unencrypted protocols the payload is the whole point: HTTP method, URL, headers, cookies, body; SMTP MAIL FROM and RCPT TO; FTP commands; DNS queries. For encrypted protocols, only metadata remains — but as we will see in Chapter 22, metadata is surprisingly expressive.

Hands-on

Run tcpdump on your own loopback to see headers:

sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -X -c 5 'tcp port 80'
# In another shell, trigger traffic:
curl http://localhost/

The -X prints the payload hex+ASCII — you should see the literal GET / request.

docs.title: Chapter 4: What is Deep Packet Inspection?
4.1 Definition
docs.text:
Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) is the practice of examining the payload of a packet — not only its headers — to determine its content, the application that produced it, and (if applicable) the action to be taken on it.

For the Layman

A shallow inspector reads the address on the envelope (“letter is going from house A to house B, room 80”). A DPI engine opens the envelope and reads enough to say “this is a video stream”, “this is a software update”, or “this is malware”.

For the Undergraduate

DPI sits between L4 firewalling and full content reconstruction. It typically includes: protocol identification, application classification, metadata extraction, and content matching against signatures. Modern DPI engines are pipelines: packet ingress \(\to\) flow tracker \(\to\) dissector \(\to\) classifier \(\to\) action.

docs.title: 4.2 A brief history
docs.text:
• 1990s: libpcap, tcpdump, and the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) make packet capture programmable.

  • 1998: Snort, the first widely used open-source IDS, introduces signature-based payload matching.

  • Early 2000s: ISPs deploy commercial DPI (Sandvine, Procera, Allot, Cisco SCE) to shape P2P traffic.

  • 2009: The l7-filter project ships kernel-level L7 classifiers for Linux iptables.

  • 2012+: ntop releases nDPI as the de-facto open source L7 classifier, used by ntopng, Suricata, and many others.

  • 2014–present: TLS adoption explodes. DPI pivots to encrypted traffic analysis (ETA) using metadata.

  • 2018+: QUIC and HTTP/3 reduce visible fields further. ML based and behavioural NDR matures.

docs.title: 4.3 Where DPI is used
docs.text:
• Security: IDS/IPS, NDR, anti-malware gateways, DLP, CASB.

  • Network operations: application-aware QoS, SD-WAN steering, link bonding, NAT traversal.

  • Carriers / ISPs: usage-based billing, throttling, parental controls, lawful intercept.

  • Compliance: PCI-DSS, HIPAA, regulated data egress.

  • Research & measurement: academic Internet measurement, CAIDA-style studies.

Caution

DPI is dual-use. The same engine that protects a corporate network can be used to censor a country or de-anonymise dissidents. Pay attention to who deploys it, why, and with what oversight.

docs.title: Chapter 5: DPI Techniques
docs.text: There are four classical families of DPI technique, often combined.

docs.title: 5.1 Port-based classification (the baseline)
docs.text: The oldest method: “TCP/80 is HTTP, TCP/443 is HTTPS”. Cheap, but easily fooled — modern apps multiplex on 443, and proxies tunnel anything.

docs.title: 5.2 Pattern / signature matching
docs.text:
Look for specific byte sequences in the payload. Snort, Suricata, and ClamAV use this heavily.

For the Undergraduate

Efficient pattern matching at line rate requires automata: Aho–Corasick (used by Snort’s full-match), Hyperscan (Intel’s SIMD-accelerated multi-regex), and DFA/NFA compilers. A modern engine compiles thousands of rules into a single state machine.

Hands-on

Inspect a Suricata rule:

alert tcp any any -> any 80 (msg:"Suspicious wget UA"; \
  content:"User-Agent|3a| Wget"; http_header; \
  classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

The content: keyword is a literal byte match; |3a| is hex for “:”.

docs.title: 5.3 Heuristic / protocol-specific dissection
docs.text: Parse the protocol enough to extract fields. Wireshark has hundreds of dissectors (one per protocol). nDPI dissects \(\sim\)300 protocols.

docs.title: 5.4 Statistical and behavioural classification
docs.text:
When payloads are encrypted, classifiers fall back on:

  • packet size distributions,

  • inter-arrival times,

  • burstiness,

  • flow duration,

  • directionality.

Joy (Cisco), nPrint, and many ML papers use these features.

docs.title: 5.5 Combined pipelines in practice
docs.text:
A real engine looks like Figure 5.1.

Figure 5.1. A typical DPI pipeline.

docs.title: 6.1 Inline (active)
docs.text: The DPI device is in the data path. It can drop or modify traffic. Used by IPS, NGFW, SSL-decrypting proxies. Risk: it is a single point of failure and adds latency.

docs.title: 6.2 Passive (out-of-band)
docs.text:
The device receives a copy via a SPAN/mirror port or a network TAP. It can only observe and alert. Lower risk, but cannot block in real time.

Figure 6.1. A passive, out-of-band DPI deployment.

docs.title: 6.3 In-host (endpoint) inspection
docs.text: A piece of software on the endpoint (EDR agent, browser, OS firewall) inspects traffic before encryption or after decryption. This is the only way to keep visibility into modern, end-to-end-encrypted applications.

docs.title: 6.4 Cloud and SASE
docs.text: Cloud workloads need DPI too. VPC traffic mirroring (AWS, GCP) and the Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) model push DPI into cloud points of presence.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Open-source DPI Engines and Libraries
7.1 nDPI – the workhorse
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/ntop/nDPI. License: LGPLv3. Languages: C with bindings.

nDPI classifies \(\sim\)300 protocols, exposes risk flags (e.g., self-signed certs, weak ciphers), and includes JA3/JA4 fingerprinting. It is embedded in ntopng, nProbe, Suricata, and many others.

Hands-on

Build and run the standalone scanner:

git clone https://github.com/ntop/nDPI
cd nDPI && ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make
./example/ndpiReader -i sample.pcap -v 2

You will see per-flow protocol classification, JA3 hashes, and risk flags.

docs.title: 7.2 libprotoident
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/wanduow/libprotoident. Lightweight L7 classifier from the WAND group at Waikato University. Looks only at the first four bytes of each direction — ideal where payload retention is restricted.

docs.title: 7.3 l7-filter (historical)
docs.text: A Linux kernel module / userspace classifier that hooked into iptables. Now mostly unmaintained, but historically important.

docs.title: 7.4 Hyperscan
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/intel/hyperscan (and the community fork Vectorscan: https://github.com/VectorCamp/vectorscan). A high-performance multi-pattern regex engine from Intel. Suricata can use it for content matching, giving multi-Gbps throughput on commodity CPUs.

docs.title: 7.5 DPDK and AF_XDP – the speed substrate
docs.text: For 10 Gbps and beyond, packet capture itself becomes the bottleneck. DPDK (https://github.com/DPDK/dpdk) bypasses the kernel for line-rate I/O. AF_XDP (Linux kernel) gives near-DPDK speed with standard sockets.

docs.title: 7.6 PF_RING and PF_RING ZC
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/ntop/PF_RING. A Linux capture framework, used by ntop tools. ZC (Zero-Copy) is the high-speed variant.

docs.title: 7.7 Joy (encrypted traffic features)
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/cisco/joy. Cisco’s research tool to extract rich flow features (including TLS) for machine learning on encrypted traffic.

docs.title: 7.8 nPrint and netML
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/nprint/nprint. nPrint converts packets into a fixed-width, ML-friendly representation (one bit per header position) so that off-the-shelf models can ingest raw network data.

docs.title: 8.1 Definition
docs.text:
Network Detection and Response is a security category that combines:

  1. continuous monitoring of network traffic (north-south and east-west);

  2. analysis using a mix of signatures, behavioural baselines, and machine learning;

  3. integrated response: alerts, automated playbooks, and (optionally) active containment.

The term was coined around 2017–2018 (Gartner “Network Traffic Analysis” became “Network Detection and Response” in 2020) to highlight that the goal is not just detection but the response loop.

For the Layman

NDR is the network’s CCTV plus an alert ops team. The cameras (sensors) record what flows through. The team (the NDR platform) watches the recording, flags strange behaviour, and either calls security or triggers an automatic response — like locking the door.

For the Undergraduate

NDR distinguishes itself from classic IDS by emphasising:

  • Behavioural analytics, not just signatures.

  • East-west visibility (lateral movement), not only perimeter.

  • Encrypted-traffic analysis through metadata.

  • Integration with EDR, SIEM, and SOAR via APIs and STIX/TAXII.

docs.title: 8.2 The NDR pipeline
docs.text:
Figure 8.1. The five stages of an NDR platform.

Collect.

Sensors are typically Zeek or Suricata processes reading from a TAP, SPAN, ERSPAN, or cloud mirror. They emit logs (Zeek TSV/JSON) and alerts (Suricata eve.json).

Enrich.

Add context: DNS resolutions, threat-intel matches (MISP, AlienVault OTX), GeoIP (MaxMind), asset inventory (CMDB).

Analyse.

Run detection logic: rule packs (Emerging Threats), behavioural baselines (e.g., “host normally talks to 12 internal hosts; this hour it talked to 480”), and ML models (e.g., DGA classifiers, beaconing detectors).

Decide.

Aggregate alerts into cases or stories, score them, and rank.

Respond.

Push to SIEM, page on-call, push firewall rules, isolate a host through EDR.

docs.title: 8.3 NDR vs. IDS vs. NTA vs. XDR
docs.text: Table 8.1. The detection-and-response zoo. Category Primary focus Typical output IDS/IPS Match known attack signatures in real time. Alerts, optional blocks. NTA Volumetric and statistical traffic analysis. Dashboards, baselines. NDR Behavioural detection + response workflows. Cases, playbooks. EDR Endpoint process / file behaviour. Endpoint isolation. XDR Cross-source correlation (NDR + EDR + cloud + identity). Unified case. SIEM Log aggregation and querying. Searches, dashboards. SOAR Playbook automation. Tickets, actions.

docs.title: 9.1 Sensors
docs.text:
The eyes of the system. The dominant open-source pair is:

  • Suricata – signature-based, multi-threaded, fast. Good at IDS/IPS, file extraction, JA3.

  • Zeek (formerly Bro) – a programmable network analyser. Produces rich logs (conn.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log, http.log).

Most modern NDR stacks run both.

docs.title: 9.2 Storage
docs.text: PCAP is heavy (\(\sim\)1 GB per 100 Mbps per minute). Production NDRs use Arkime (formerly Moloch) for full-packet retention and a columnar store (ClickHouse, OpenSearch, or Elasticsearch) for logs.

docs.title: 9.3 Analytics
docs.text:
Three layers:

  1. Rules: ET Open, ET Pro, custom Suricata/Zeek scripts.

  2. Baselines: per-host, per-service, per-time-of-day.

  3. ML: DGA detection, beaconing, lateral-movement graphs.

docs.title: 9.4 Response
docs.text:
• Push to a SIEM (Wazuh, Splunk, Elastic SIEM).

  • Trigger SOAR playbooks (Shuffle, TheHive + Cortex).

  • Quarantine a host via the EDR API (Velociraptor, OSQuery).

docs.title: 9.5 An open-source NDR reference stack
docs.text: Figure 9.1. An entirely open-source NDR stack – often shipped as Security Onion.

docs.title: 10.1 Where ML adds value
docs.text:
• DGA (Domain Generation Algorithm) detection: classifying domain names that look algorithmically generated.

  • Beacon detection: spotting periodic, low-volume callbacks characteristic of C2 (Cobalt Strike, Sliver).

  • Encrypted malware classification: features over TLS handshake + packet timing.

  • Lateral movement graphs: anomalies in host-to-host edge formation.

docs.title: 10.2 Open datasets
docs.text:
• CICIDS-2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018 – University of New Brunswick. https://www.unb.ca/cic/datasets/

  • CTU-13 – botnet captures.

  • Stratosphere IPS labs – malware PCAPs. https://www.stratosphereips.org/datasets-overview

  • MAWILab – Japanese backbone traces with anomaly labels.

docs.title: 10.3 Open ML-for-network projects
docs.text:
• Stratosphere Linux IPS (Slips): https://github.com/stratosphereips/StratosphereLinuxIPS.

  • AI-Hunter (community Rita-based).

  • Malcolm (CISA’s open NDR/PCAP analysis platform): https://github.com/cisagov/Malcolm.

  • nPrintML: combining nPrint with AutoML.

For the Undergraduate

A typical pipeline: take the first \(N\) packets of each flow, extract a fixed feature vector (sizes, IATs, TLS handshake bytes), train a gradient boosted tree or a 1-D CNN. Beware concept drift: signatures of benign traffic shift as web technologies evolve, so retraining quarterly is normal.

docs.title: Chapter 11: IDS and IPS
docs.text: An Intrusion Detection System watches and alerts. An Intrusion Prevention System watches and blocks. Both rely on the same engines; only deployment differs.

docs.title: 11.1 The three classical engines
docs.text:
• Snort – https://github.com/snort3/snort3. The original, Cisco-stewarded. Rule language is the lingua franca.

  • Suricata – https://github.com/OISF/suricata. Multi-threaded, modern, Snort-compatible rules.

  • Zeek – https://github.com/zeek/zeek. Not a signature engine; a programmable analyser. Often paired with Suricata.

docs.title: 11.2 Rule packs
docs.text:
• Emerging Threats Open (ET Open) – free. https://rules.emergingthreats.net/open/

  • ET Pro – commercial.

  • Snort Subscriber (Talos) – commercial.

  • Custom rules from CERTs and your own SOC.

docs.title: 11.3 Anatomy of a Suricata rule
docs.text:
alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (
  msg:"ET POLICY curl User-Agent Outbound";
  flow:established,to_server;
  http.user_agent; content:"curl/";
  classtype:policy-violation;
  sid:2013505; rev:3;
  metadata:created_at 2011_10_20;
)

docs.title: 11.4 Tuning the alert flood
docs.text:
A new IDS will drown a SOC. The standard treatments:

  • Disable noisy rules per environment (suricata-update disable-conf).

  • Threshold/suppress per source.

  • Push only high-fidelity alerts to humans; everything else into the warehouse for hunting.

docs.title: Chapter 12: NTA, NPM, and Flow Analytics
docs.text:
NTA (Network Traffic Analysis) is the older sibling of NDR. It focuses on flows and volumes more than on threats.

NPM (Network Performance Monitoring) is operations-oriented: latency, jitter, packet loss, application response time.

Both rely on:

  • NetFlow (Cisco): summary records exported by routers.

  • IPFIX (RFC 7011): the standardised successor.

  • sFlow: packet-sampling-based, vendor-neutral.

docs.title: 12.1 Open tools
docs.text:
• nfdump / nfsen – classic NetFlow toolset.

  • ntopng – https://github.com/ntop/ntopng. Real-time, rich web UI, uses nDPI.

  • Akvorado – https://github.com/akvorado/akvorado. Modern flow visualiser by Free Mobile.

  • ElastiFlow – commercial+free Elastic-based dashboards.

  • Pmacct – aggregator, exporter, BGP correlator.

docs.title: 13.1 SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)
docs.text:
A log warehouse + alerting engine. Examples:

  • Wazuh (open source) – https://github.com/wazuh/wazuh.

  • Elastic Security – open core.

  • Splunk, IBM QRadar, Microsoft Sentinel – commercial.

docs.title: 13.2 SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response)
docs.text:
Runs playbooks across tools.

  • Shuffle – https://github.com/Shuffle/Shuffle.

  • TheHive + Cortex – https://github.com/TheHive-Project.

docs.title: 13.3 EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)
docs.text: Watches processes, file system, and registry on endpoints. Examples: Velociraptor (https://github.com/Velocidex/velociraptor), OSQuery (https://github.com/osquery/osquery), Wazuh (also doubles as EDR), and commercial CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

docs.title: 13.4 XDR (eXtended Detection and Response)
docs.text: A platform that fuses NDR + EDR + cloud + identity signals into a single case. Sometimes a marketing label, sometimes a real product.

docs.title: 13.5 How they relate
docs.text: Figure 13.1. Signal sources feed correlation; correlation drives automation.

docs.title: 13.6 Threat intel: MISP and OpenCTI
docs.text:
NDR/IDS without intel is half-blind. The community-standard platforms:

  • MISP – https://github.com/MISP/MISP. Shares IOCs (IPs, hashes, domains, YARA, Sigma) across organisations.

  • OpenCTI – https://github.com/OpenCTI-Platform/opencti. Knowledge-graph oriented; great for adversary tracking.

  • STIX/TAXII – the standards (MITRE).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Wireshark, tshark, and tcpdump
docs.text: These are the three most important commands a network professional learns.

docs.title: 14.1 tcpdump
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump. The original CLI capture tool. Built on libpcap.

Hands-on

Cheat-sheet:

# Capture 100 packets on eth0, save to file
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 -w cap.pcap

# Only DNS traffic, verbose
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -vv 'udp port 53'

# All traffic to/from a host on a specific port
sudo tcpdump -nn 'host 1.2.3.4 and tcp port 443'

# Show payload as hex+ASCII
sudo tcpdump -nn -X -c 5 'tcp port 80'

# Read from file, filter further
tcpdump -r cap.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'

docs.title: 14.2 Wireshark
docs.text:
Project: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark (mirror at https://github.com/wireshark/wireshark). The GUI. Has \(\sim\)3000 protocol dissectors, follow-TCP-stream, TLS decryption with a keylog file, statistics galore. The display-filter language differs from BPF capture filters:

# Capture filter (BPF, libpcap):
tcp port 443 and host 1.2.3.4

# Display filter (Wireshark):
tls.handshake.extensions_server_name == "example.com"

docs.title: 14.3 tshark
docs.text:
The headless Wireshark. Perfect for scripts.

# Extract every SNI and the source IP
tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'tls.handshake.type==1' \
  -T fields -e ip.src -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name

# Print HTTP requests with method + host + URI
tshark -r cap.pcap -Y http.request \
  -T fields -e http.request.method -e http.host -e http.request.uri

docs.title: 14.4 Decrypting TLS for inspection
docs.text:
With control of the client, set:

export SSLKEYLOGFILE=/tmp/keys.log
firefox &  # writes ephemeral TLS secrets to that file

Then point Wireshark to keys.log (Preferences \(\to\) Protocols \(\to\) TLS \(\to\) (Pre)-Master-Secret log filename) and the handshakes become readable.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Zeek
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/zeek/zeek. License: BSD.

Zeek is a domain-specific programming language and runtime, not just a sniffer. By default it produces structured logs of everything worth knowing:

  • conn.log – every TCP/UDP connection,

  • dns.log – every DNS query and reply,

  • http.log – every HTTP transaction (cleartext),

  • ssl.log – every TLS handshake (SNI, cert, JA3),

  • x509.log – every certificate seen,

  • files.log – every file traversal,

  • notice.log – alerts and policy events,

and many more. A single Zeek log line is often more useful than 1,000 PCAP packets.

Hands-on

Run Zeek over a pcap:

zeek -r capture.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T
ls -1 *.log
jq -r '.id_orig_h+" -> "+.id_resp_h+" "+(.service//"-")' conn.log | head

docs.title: 15.1 Writing a Zeek script
docs.text:
Detect domains shorter than 5 chars (toy example):

event dns_request(c: connection, msg: dns_msg, query: string,
                  qtype: count, qclass: count)
  {
  if ( |query| < 5 )
    NOTICE([$note=DNS::Suspicious_Short_Query,
            $msg=fmt("short DNS query:
            $conn=c]);
  }

docs.title: 15.2 Useful Zeek packages
docs.text:
• zeek-EternalSafety – ETERNAL* exploit detection.

  • zeek-sniffpass – detects HTTP form passwords.

  • ja3-zeek – adds JA3/JA3S/JA4 fingerprints.

  • zeek-bro-pkg-manager (zkg) – the package manager.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Suricata in depth
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/OISF/suricata. License: GPLv2.

Suricata is a multi-threaded IDS/IPS/NSM engine.

docs.title: 16.1 Output streams
docs.text:
• eve.json – a unified JSON event stream (alerts, flows, DNS, HTTP, TLS, files, anomalies).

  • fast.log – short alert lines for humans.

  • stats.log – counters.

  • Extracted files into a directory.

docs.title: 16.2 Anatomy of eve.json
docs.text:
{"timestamp":"2026-05-15T10:00:00Z","event_type":"alert",
 "src_ip":"10.0.0.5","dest_ip":"45.55.10.2","src_port":58122,
 "dest_port":443,"proto":"TCP",
 "alert":{"signature_id":2027757,
   "signature":"ET MALWARE Cobalt Strike Beacon",
   "category":"A Network Trojan was detected","severity":1},
 "tls":{"sni":"cdn-evil.example","ja3":{"hash":"e7d705a3286e..."}}}

docs.title: 16.3 IPS mode (inline)
docs.text:
On Linux with nfqueue:

sudo iptables -I FORWARD -j NFQUEUE --queue-num 0
sudo suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -q 0

docs.title: 16.4 Rule management
docs.text:
sudo suricata-update                            # default: ET Open
sudo suricata-update list-sources
sudo suricata-update enable-source et/open
sudo suricata-update disable-sid 2013505
sudo systemctl reload suricata

docs.title: Chapter 17: Snort 3
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/snort3/snort3.

Snort 3 is a rewrite of the original Snort. Key concepts:

  • Modules (LuaJIT-configurable).

  • Inspectors (per-protocol).

  • Hyperscan for pattern matching.

  • Appid for application identification.

Rule language is mostly Snort 2 compatible.

snort -c /etc/snort/snort.lua -R /etc/snort/rules/local.rules \
      -r capture.pcap -A alert_fast

docs.title: Chapter 18: Arkime, RITA, Malcolm, and Security Onion
18.1 Arkime (formerly Moloch)
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/arkime/arkime. Full-packet capture with web search. Indexes flow metadata in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch; raw PCAPs stay on disk. A defender’s time machine.

docs.title: 18.2 RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics)
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/activecm/rita. Consumes Zeek logs and runs offline analytics: beaconing, long connections, DNS tunnelling. Now succeeded by AC-Hunter Community.

docs.title: 18.3 Malcolm
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/cisagov/Malcolm. CISA’s open-source NDR. Bundles Arkime, Zeek, Suricata, OpenSearch, and dashboards into Docker Compose. Great for ICS/OT visibility.

docs.title: 18.4 Security Onion
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/Security-Onion-Solutions/securityonion. A complete NDR/SIEM distribution. Includes Zeek, Suricata, Strelka, Stenographer (full PCAP), Elastic, Kibana, TheHive, Cortex, Velociraptor.

docs.title: 18.5 Stenographer
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/google/stenographer. Google’s open-source full-PCAP recorder optimised for fast lookups.

docs.title: Chapter 19: ntop family
docs.text:
ntop is a Pisa-based group with one of the most complete network monitoring portfolios. All open core.

  • ntopng – https://github.com/ntop/ntopng: live web dashboard, uses nDPI.

  • nProbe – flow exporter, embeds nDPI, JA3/JA4.

  • n2disk – 100 Gbps full-packet recording.

  • PF_RING – packet I/O framework.

  • nDPI – the protocol classifier (Chapter 7).

Hands-on

Spin up ntopng in Docker for a quick look:

docker run --rm --net=host -it ntop/ntopng:stable -i eth0 -W 3000
# Then visit http://localhost:3000  (default admin/admin)

docs.title: Chapter 20: Signature-based Detection
docs.text: A signature is a precise description of a known bad thing. Strengths: high precision, easy explanations. Weaknesses: no help against unknown attacks, easy to evade by trivial mutation.

docs.title: 20.1 Anatomy of a payload signature
docs.text:
The Snort/Suricata syntax (simplified):

ACTION PROTO SRC SPORT -> DST DPORT (OPTIONS;)

Options include content, pcre, flow, sticky buffers (http.uri, http.header, tls.sni, dns.query), threshold, flowbits, classtype, sid, rev.

docs.title: 20.2 Sticky buffers, the modern best practice
docs.text:
Instead of inspecting the raw packet, modern rules say “this match is inside the URI” or “inside the TLS SNI”. This is much faster and more precise:

alert tls any any -> any any (
  msg:"Self-signed cert with known evil CN";
  tls.cert_subject; content:"CN=evil-corp";
  flow:established,to_client;
  sid:1000010;)

docs.title: 20.3 YARA – a sibling for files
docs.text:
Project: https://github.com/VirusTotal/yara. YARA is to files what Suricata is to packets: a pattern-matching DSL. Suricata + Zeek extract files; YARA scans them.

rule SuspiciousPowerShell {
  strings:
    $a = "FromBase64String"
    $b = "Invoke-Expression"
    $c = "DownloadString"
  condition:
    2 of them
}

docs.title: 20.4 Sigma – vendor-neutral detections
docs.text: Project: https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma. A YAML format for detections that can be translated to Splunk, Elastic, QRadar, Sentinel queries.

docs.title: 21.1 Why
docs.text: Signatures cannot describe what we have never seen. Behavioural detection asks: “does this host behave like itself?” or “does this flow look like any flow this network has seen before?”

docs.title: 21.2 Common techniques
docs.text:
• Statistical baselining: per-host bytes/hour distribution, per-port connection count. Z-scores or robust quantiles.

  • Beacon detection: look at the periodicity of small connections to the same destination. A C2 beacon at 60-second intervals stands out from organic browsing.

  • DGA detection: classify domain names with \(n\)-gram models or character LSTMs.

  • Lateral movement graphs: model host-to-host edges as a graph; raise alerts when a host suddenly creates many new edges.

  • Frequency / rarity: “how rare is this user-agent on this network?”

docs.title: 21.3 An example beacon detector in pseudocode
docs.text:
for each (src, dst, port) flow group F over the last 24h:
    times  = sorted timestamps in F
    deltas = differences between consecutive times
    if len(deltas) > 20 and stddev(deltas)/mean(deltas) < 0.1:
        emit("beacon-like", src, dst, port, mean(deltas))

This is essentially what RITA and AC-Hunter do, with refinements.

docs.title: 21.4 Graph-based detection
docs.text: Cast traffic as a graph: nodes are hosts, edges are connections weighted by bytes or flow count. Apply community detection, PageRank, or graph neural networks to find oddities. Open-source projects: PyGraphistry, Stellargraph, Cuwhisker.

docs.title: Chapter 22: Encrypted Traffic Analysis (ETA)
docs.text: When everything is encrypted, the inspector must work with what is left: handshake metadata, packet sizes, timing, certificate features, and domain reputation.

docs.title: 22.1 TLS fingerprints
docs.text:
JA3 / JA3S.

A hash of selected ClientHello (JA3) and ServerHello (JA3S) fields. Two clients with the same TLS stack and configuration produce the same JA3. Project: https://github.com/salesforce/ja3.

JA4 / JA4+.

A FoxIO-led successor, more robust to TLS 1.3 field randomisation, with per-protocol variants (JA4S, JA4H for HTTP, JA4X for X.509, JA4L for latency). Project: https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/ja4.

HASSH.

Equivalent fingerprint for SSH. Project: https://github.com/salesforce/hassh.

TLS GREASE.

Random values inserted by clients to ensure servers tolerate unknown values. JA3 is sensitive to GREASE; JA4 is not.

docs.title: 22.2 Domain reputation & DNS analytics
docs.text:
• Newly Registered Domains (NRDs) feeds.

  • Passive DNS (Farsight DNSDB, Mnemonic).

  • DNS over HTTPS (DoH) / DNS over TLS (DoT) – hides queries from the local resolver but leaves a TLS handshake to the DoH provider, which can itself be fingerprinted.

docs.title: 22.3 Certificate analytics
docs.text: A self-signed or recently issued (Let’s Encrypt) cert plus a fresh domain plus a high-entropy SNI = classic C2 setup. ssl-anomaly Zeek package flags this in seconds.

docs.title: 22.4 Cisco’s ETA approach
docs.text:
Cisco published the Encrypted Traffic Analytics approach using:

  • the Initial Data Packet (IDP) – first 1500 bytes,

  • the Sequence of Packet Lengths and Times (SPLT),

  • byte distribution of unencrypted bytes.

Joy (Section 7) exposes these features.

docs.title: 23.1 The hunter’s mindset
docs.text: A hunt is a hypothesis-driven search through past data: “has host X ever talked to a known C2 IP since 90 days ago?”, “were there DNS queries with \(>\)200 byte responses?”, “which TLS handshakes used an outdated cipher?” Hunting is the bread and butter of a mature SOC.

docs.title: 23.2 Common Zeek-log hunts
docs.text:
# Top 10 talkers by bytes
jq -s 'group_by(.id_orig_h)
       | map({h:.[0].id_orig_h, b:map(.orig_ip_bytes)|add})
       | sort_by(-.b)[:10]' conn.log

# All TLS handshakes to short, alphabetic SNIs
jq -r 'select(.server_name|test("^[a-z]{1,5}\\.[a-z]{2,4}$"))
       | [.id_orig_h, .server_name] | @tsv' ssl.log

# DNS queries with TXT replies of large size
jq -r 'select(.qtype_name=="TXT" and (.answers|length)>0)
       | [.id_orig_h, .query, (.answers|length)] | @tsv' dns.log

docs.title: 23.3 PCAP carving with Zeek and tshark
docs.text:
Extracting downloaded files:

zeek -r capture.pcap LocalFile::extract_dir=./extracted
ls extracted/
file extracted/*

docs.title: Chapter 24: Lab 1: Capture, Open, Inspect
docs.text:
Goal: capture five minutes of your own traffic and open it.

Hands-on

# 1. Pick an interface
ip -br link

# 2. Capture (Linux/macOS)
sudo tcpdump -i wlan0 -w lab1.pcap -G 300 -W 1

# 3. Open the result
wireshark lab1.pcap

In Wireshark try the filters: tls.handshake.type==1, dns, http.request, and Statistics \(\to\) Conversations.

docs.title: Chapter 25: Lab 2: Build a Mini-NDR with Docker
docs.text:
Hands-on

# Get a sample PCAP
curl -O https://www.malware-traffic-analysis.net/2024/sample.pcap

# Run Zeek
docker run --rm -v $PWD:/data zeek/zeek:lts \
  zeek -r /data/sample.pcap LogAscii::use_json=T

# Run Suricata
docker run --rm -v $PWD:/data \
  jasonish/suricata:latest -r /data/sample.pcap \
  --set "outputs.0.fast.enabled=yes"

You will have conn.log, dns.log, etc. alongside eve.json and fast.log.

docs.title: Chapter 26: Lab 3: A Suricata Rule from Scratch
docs.text:
Goal: alert on outgoing connections to any .zip download whose host header contains a numeric IP.

alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (
  msg:"POLICY ZIP download from numeric host";
  flow:to_server,established;
  http.method; content:"GET";
  http.uri; content:".zip"; endswith; nocase;
  http.host; pcre:"/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+/";
  classtype:policy-violation;
  sid:1000020; rev:1;)

Drop this into /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules, reload, and test with curl http://1.2.3.4/test.zip.

docs.title: Chapter 27: Lab 4: Beacon Detection with RITA
docs.text:
Hands-on

# Install RITA + Zeek (Linux x86_64)
git clone https://github.com/activecm/rita
cd rita && ./install.sh

# Ingest Zeek logs
rita import /opt/zeek/logs/2026-05-15 lab-db
rita show-beacons lab-db | head

You will see (src, dst, score) triples; the highest scores are the most beacon-like flows.

docs.title: Chapter 28: Lab 5: JA3 Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Hands-on

# Install ja3
git clone https://github.com/salesforce/ja3
cd ja3/python
python3 ja3.py -a sample.pcap

Each TLS handshake gets a JA3 hash; compare your browser’s hash to the public lists at https://sslbl.abuse.ch/ja3-fingerprints/.

docs.title: Chapter 29: Lab 6: Building a JA4 Profile of Your Network
docs.text:
Hands-on

# Suricata 7+ supports JA4 natively
suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml \
  --set "app-layer.protocols.tls.ja4.enabled=yes" \
  -r capture.pcap

# Extract JA4 hashes from eve.json
jq -r '.tls?.ja4?' eve.json | sort -u | head

docs.title: 30.1 The legal landscape
docs.text:
DPI inspects content. Content inspection is regulated. A non-exhaustive list of legal frameworks that may apply:

  • EU/EEA: GDPR (data protection), ePrivacy (communications confidentiality).

  • USA: Wiretap Act (18 U.S.C. § 2510), Stored Communications Act, CALEA, state laws.

  • India: IT Act 2000 (Section 69), DPDP Act 2023.

  • UK: Investigatory Powers Act 2016.

  • Sectoral: HIPAA (US health), PCI-DSS (payments), MAS-TRM (Singapore finance).

The common thread: you may inspect traffic on networks you own with the informed consent (often via acceptable-use policy) of users, and with proper safeguards.

docs.title: 30.2 The ethical landscape
docs.text:
• Minimise what you collect; retain only what you need.

  • Encrypt and access-control captures; PCAP is treasure for an attacker.

  • Document why each rule exists; tune away anything that unnecessarily exposes personal life details.

  • Be transparent with users; surveillance without consent corrodes trust.

Caution

DPI techniques can be turned to censorship, traffic discrimination, or political surveillance. The same nDPI that protects a hospital can be deployed by an authoritarian ISP. As an engineer you carry the responsibility for how you deploy the tool, regardless of the manufacturer’s intent.

docs.title: 31.1 Where the bottlenecks live
docs.text:
1. NIC to kernel: interrupts, RSS, ring buffers.

  2. Kernel to user: socket overhead, copies.

  3. Decode: protocol dissection.

  4. Match: regex / Aho-Corasick.

  5. Write: log volume.

docs.title: 31.2 Modern accelerators
docs.text:
• AF_PACKET v3 + fanout – baseline Linux.

  • AF_XDP – bypasses skb, near zero-copy.

  • DPDK – userspace polling drivers.

  • PF_RING ZC – ntop’s userspace ring.

  • Hyperscan / Vectorscan – SIMD regex.

  • eBPF + XDP – in-kernel filtering before the rest of the stack sees the packet.

  • SmartNICs / DPUs – offload classification.

docs.title: 31.3 Sizing rules of thumb
docs.text:
• One modern x86 core can typically handle 1–2 Gbps of Suricata with full rules.

  • Zeek scales with cores via cluster mode; budget \(\sim\)500 Mbps per worker.

  • Full PCAP at 10 Gbps for a week needs \(\sim\)110 TB of storage.

  • Mirror ports drop silently when saturated; TAPs do not.

docs.title: Chapter 32: The Future: QUIC, ECH, AI, and the Encrypted Internet
32.1 QUIC and HTTP/3
docs.text:
QUIC encrypts almost everything once unique to TCP+TLS: handshake fields, connection migration, multiplexing. Long-term, classical DPI will only see:

  • the QUIC Initial packet (still partially visible),

  • SNI (until ECH is rolled out),

  • destination IP and port,

  • packet sizes and timing.

Adapt or die: every modern NDR must support QUIC flow tracking.

docs.title: 32.2 Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)
docs.text: ECH wraps the SNI inside an encrypted blob using a key fetched from DNS HTTPS records. When it is widely deployed, SNI-based filtering ends. The arms race moves to DNS analytics, certificate transparency, and behavioural inference.

docs.title: 32.3 AI / LLMs in NDR
docs.text:
Three concrete uses are emerging:

  1. Alert summarisation: turn dozens of NDR alerts into a narrative for a tier-1 analyst.

  2. Rule and detection generation: “write me a Suricata rule for X”.

  3. Reasoning over Zeek logs: chat with your traffic logs.

Open work to watch: ML-based DGA classifiers built on transformers; HuggingFace models for log anomaly detection; the LLM4Sec community.

docs.title: 32.4 The long arc
docs.text: DPI is a moving frontier. Twenty years ago a payload regex was state of the art; today the same regex is bypassed by TLS in five minutes. The constant is visibility: as long as networks move data, somebody will want to know what is moving and why. The tools, names, and acronyms change; the discipline endures.

docs.title: Closing Note
docs.text: The wire is honest in a way few other surfaces are: bits either arrive or they do not, and once they have arrived they cannot lie about what they are. Encryption hides their content, not their existence. As long as humans care what their networks are doing — to defend, to operate, to research, to comply — there will be a craft of looking carefully at packets. May this book be a useful early map of that craft.
